questions.scenario: A finance coordinator must send a letter to a customer explaining why a refund of £148.60 was delayed and will now be processed next working day. The letter will be read by the customer and may be forwarded to their bank. Her draft prompt says: 'Write a polite explanation about a refund delay.'
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement to the prompt?

options.text: Name the audience and what they need to do with the letter, the specific facts to state, and the tone to use — a calm, factual, non-technical register suitable for something a customer may forward to their bank.
Add more context about the refund process, so Claude has more to write about.
Ask for a shorter letter, since politeness and length trade off against each other.
Paste two example letters the company has sent before, so Claude can match their tone.

questions.explanation: The prompt names a task and a manner but none of the **constraints Claude cannot infer**: who reads this, what they must be able to do afterwards, which facts have to appear, and in what register. Stating those is what turns a polite letter into one that is correct, forwardable and appropriately formal. Examples are a strong addition and worth pairing with this — but they cannot supply the facts or the audience, which is the gap here.

whyWrong.B: More background about the process does not tell Claude what this particular letter has to say or who has to be able to use it. The missing content is the audience and the required facts, not process detail.
whyWrong.C: Brevity is not the problem, and cutting length can remove the specific facts a forwarded letter needs to be useful. Nothing in the prompt currently says what has to be included.
whyWrong.D: Examples are worth adding and would help with tone — but they cannot tell Claude this refund's amount, this delay and this next-step date. Those have to be in the prompt.

questions.mindset: A task and a manner are not constraints — name the audience, the required facts and the register.

questions.scenario: A council's communications officer writes public notices. Her requests usually begin 'write a notice about'. Responses are consistently too long, use technical language, and omit the date by which people must respond — a legal requirement for this type of notice.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: State the constraints the model cannot infer: the reading level, the maximum length, the required structure including the response deadline, and the rule that anything else goes in the attached explanation rather than the notice.
Specify the model to use, since the tier is the reason the responses are too long.
Ask for the notice to be written in a formal legal register, since public notices should sound official.
Cut each request down to its essentials, so the prompt itself is shorter and the response follows it.

questions.explanation: The symptoms all point at the same cause — **unstated constraints** — and one of them is a legal requirement being missed. The reader, the length, the required structure including the response date, and where detail belongs are all things Claude cannot work out from 'write a notice about'. Making the deadline a required structural element is what guarantees it appears rather than depending on how the notice is phrased that day.

whyWrong.B: Model tier does not affect whether a legal requirement is met. The deadline is absent because nothing in the request makes it part of the notice's structure.
whyWrong.C: A more formal register would make the notice harder to read, which is one of the existing problems. Official-sounding is not the requirement; readable, complete and correctly structured is.
whyWrong.D: Shorter requests do not fix missing content — they remove even less. The request is already short, and length is not what is wrong with it.

questions.mindset: When responses consistently miss something required, make it a structural element of the requested output rather than a hope about wording.

questions.scenario: A support lead writes one prompt used by 40 agents to draft replies to customers reporting the same three service issues. Some agents type extra instructions into their requests, others do not. Replies vary in length and structure, and one of the three issue types consistently gets a reply that omits the escalation steps.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: Move the shared rules — structure, length, and the escalation steps for each of the three issue types — into the Project's instructions, so they apply to every reply regardless of who types the request.
Ask the agents who are getting the omission to add a reminder to their own requests until the issue is resolved.
Ask for the three reply types to be written as three separate prompts, so agents choose the right one each time.
Include a worked example of a correct reply for the issue type that keeps omitting the escalation steps.

questions.explanation: The rule that keeps being missed is a rule that **somebody has to remember to type**, and forty people will remember it inconsistently. Because it holds for every reply of that type, it belongs in shared configuration that applies automatically — which is what stops the omission depending on which agent was on shift. A worked example is a good complement and may well be added, but it demonstrates the shape of a reply rather than guaranteeing a required step appears in all of them.

whyWrong.B: This fixes the symptom for the agents who noticed and leaves the rule dependent on typing. The omission will recur on the shift where nobody adds the reminder.
whyWrong.C: Three prompts means three sets of instructions to keep in step and a choice for every reply. One prompt with the rules in shared configuration is less to maintain and cannot be used incorrectly by omission.
whyWrong.D: A worked example is a genuine improvement and would show what a compliant reply looks like. It does not guarantee the escalation steps appear in every reply, which is what the failure requires.

questions.mindset: A rule that must always apply belongs where it applies automatically, not in requests people have to remember to type.

questions.scenario: An HR assistant builds a reusable prompt for drafting interview questions for any role. Her prompt says 'ask good questions' and 'cover the important stuff'. She notices drafts that are technically fine but ask about teamwork for a role whose entire job is solitary fieldwork.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: Name the constraints: questions must be answerable from the candidate's own experience, must probe at least two levels beyond surface detail, must be phrased so a strong candidate and a weak one would give visibly different answers, and must avoid assuming anything not in the role description.
Ask for the questions in numbered lists, since formatting is what makes drafts usable.
Add the job descriptions for five common roles as examples, so Claude can see the pattern.
Ask Claude to ask the hiring manager for more detail before producing questions, so the requests are self-correcting.

questions.explanation: 'Good questions' and 'the important stuff' leave every decision open, so the model supplies its own defaults — which is why a solitary role gets teamwork questions. What was missing is the **test a question has to pass**: answerable from real experience, probing beyond the surface, separating a strong from a weak candidate, and not importing assumptions from outside the role description. Stating those makes the prompt reusable across roles, which is the whole point of building it.

whyWrong.B: Numbering changes presentation and does nothing about content. The problem is which questions get asked, not how they are laid out.
whyWrong.C: Five job descriptions would help Claude see the pattern, but the pattern would be inferred from examples rather than stated, so it will not transfer reliably to the sixth role — and the requirement is that it does.
whyWrong.D: Asking for more detail is reasonable when the role description is thin, and it makes the requests longer for every user. It does not fix the case described, where the information was available but nothing said what a good question required.

questions.mindset: A reusable prompt needs the test each output must pass, stated as criteria — adjectives like 'good' hand every decision back to the model.

questions.scenario: A marketing coordinator writes product descriptions for a range of homeware. Her prompt is 'Write a product description for this item: [item details]', with no other instruction. Descriptions arrive well written but about 200 words long, in a single flowing paragraph, and each one opens by describing the room the product would suit.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: State the required structure — the specific attributes in a fixed order, then a short use sentence, then a closing line — with the length specified.
Give three worked examples of descriptions that are right, so the pattern is visible.
Ask for the tone to be 'warm and evocative', since the current descriptions are too dry and technical.
Move each product's details into the request as a labelled table of attributes, so the model has the facts in a consistent form.

questions.explanation: The description is a **template the request does not specify**, and every default has filled the same gap: a long single paragraph, and an opening about the room because nothing said the attributes must lead. A stated structure with a length fixes the shape directly, and worked examples show it — the two are strongest together, since the rule tells Claude what to do and the examples show what it looks like. The tone request is worth noting as a misdiagnosis: the problem is not dryness.

whyWrong.C: The descriptions are not dry or technical — they open with a sentence about decor. The issue is structure and length, and asking for a warmer register would push further towards the opening line that is already wrong.
whyWrong.D: Presenting facts consistently is good hygiene, but the item details were already supplied and the model had enough to work with. The unstated requirement was the shape of the output, not the form of the input.

questions.mindset: When outputs have the wrong shape, specify the structure and show a worked example — asking for a different tone treats the wrong symptom.

questions.scenario: A charity's finance lead has decomposed month-end board reporting into three steps: pull the figures from three accounting exports, write the commentary explaining variances, and format the pack. Step one produces plausible numbers that are sometimes wrong. Step three works well.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions would MOST improve this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Make step one verify itself: ask for each figure to be reported with the export file, sheet and cell it came from, so wrong values are visible at the point they enter.
Merge steps one and two into a single request, so the commentary and the figures are produced together and stay consistent.
Check a sample of step-one figures against the exports before step two runs, so an error is found before it reaches the board pack.
Rewrite step three to include the verification, since formatting is where the pack is assembled.

questions.explanation: Wrong figures entering at step one will be faithfully carried through the rest, so the fix belongs **at the point of entry**. Requiring a source reference for each figure makes an error visible immediately, and checking a sample before the commentary step catches anything that got through. Merging the steps would actually make the problem worse, because a plausible commentary written around a wrong figure is harder to notice than a bare number.

whyWrong.B: This removes the checkpoint rather than strengthening it. Figures and narrative produced together is precisely the case where a wrong figure looks justified by a fluent explanation around it.
whyWrong.D: Formatting is where the pack is assembled, not where the values are read. Verification has to happen before the commentary explains those values, or it is verifying a claim already made.

questions.mindset: Put verification at the point where the value enters the workflow, before anything interprets or explains it.

questions.scenario: A bid manager must produce a first-draft tender response from four documents: a 90-page technical specification, a 40-page compliance schedule, the client's own 20-page brief and last year's winning response. She has one week and no other resource.
questions.stem: Which breakdown would MOST improve her chances of a usable draft?

options.text: Step one: extract every requirement from the technical specification as a numbered list with the clause it comes from. Step two: do the same for the compliance schedule. Step three: match both lists against the brief and flag anything not addressed. Step four: draft the response from the verified list.
Step one: draft the response sections one at a time, reading the relevant part of the specification before each. Step two: check the compliance schedule. Step three: send it.
Ask Claude to read all four documents and produce the full response, then review each section against the specification.
Step one: summarise the client's brief. Step two: ask Claude to write the response in the same structure as last year's winning answer.

questions.explanation: This is a **verification problem before a writing problem**, and that ordering is the whole difference. Extracting requirements with their source clause creates a checklist that can be checked against what was actually written, and the match step finds what is missing while it is still cheap to fix. Writing first and checking after means the omissions are discovered in a finished document, which is the expensive place to find them — and matching an old bid's structure assumes last year's scope is this year's.

whyWrong.B: Drafting section by section interleaves reading and writing, so nothing is held as a checklist. Nothing in this structure guarantees that a requirement was noticed at all, which is the failure mode the specification invites.
whyWrong.C: This inverts the dependency: the review at the end is the only completeness check, on a long finished document, with no list to check it against. It is also the option most likely to produce confident content drawn from the wrong document.
whyWrong.D: Matching last year's winning response transfers its structure and assumes its scope. The specification and compliance schedule are what determine what must be answered this time.

questions.mindset: For work that must satisfy a specification, extract and check requirements before writing, not after.

questions.scenario: A customer-success manager has a vague instruction from her director: 'improve how we handle renewals.' She is not sure whether this means the email, the process, the timing, or the escalation path, and she has an afternoon to produce something useful.
questions.stem: Which TWO approaches would BEST serve her? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to help turn the vague brief into a set of specific testable requirements — what 'better' would mean, measured how, and by when — before doing any of the work.
Draft an improved renewal email immediately, since the email is the most visible part of the process.
Ask the director three questions that turn 'improve renewals' into something decidable: which stage, which measure, and what deadline.
Survey the team about what frustrates them most about renewals, and act on whichever issue comes first.

questions.explanation: A vague brief produces vague output, so the first job is to **make the ask decidable before starting the work**. Turning it into specific, testable requirements tells her what 'better' means and how anyone would know; asking the director the three questions that resolve stage, measure and deadline gets the answer from the person who owns the decision. Both are cheap and both prevent an afternoon spent polishing the wrong thing.

whyWrong.B: Improving the most visible part of a process the director did not specify is a guess. If the real problem is escalation timing, a better email achieves nothing and reports success.
whyWrong.D: Team frustration is useful evidence and it is not the same as the director's objective. Acting on whichever issue surfaces first is still choosing without knowing what 'better' was meant to mean.

questions.mindset: A vague brief needs to become testable requirements before any work starts — polish on an undefined goal is wasted effort.

questions.scenario: A training coordinator has a prompt that produces good end-of-session feedback forms. After two rounds she has added 'be specific' — and the forms now contain invented specifics: training-room details, module names and scores that were never provided.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely explanation and the BEST fix?

options.text: 'Be specific' asks for detail the request does not contain, so the model supplies plausible detail. Replace it with an explicit rule that anything not supplied is left blank or marked as unknown.
The forms are too long, so shorten them and the invented details will stop appearing.
Use a more capable model, since inventing details to satisfy 'be specific' is a reasoning limitation.
Add the missing training details to the request each time, so the specific content is always available.

questions.explanation: 'Be specific' is a request for detail **without a source**, and the model fills the gap with plausible detail. The two words are doing the opposite of what was intended: they are inviting invention. The fix is to say what to do when information is missing — leave it blank, or mark it as not supplied — which converts a licence to invent into a defined behaviour. The rest of the prompt was working; one adjective removed it.

whyWrong.B: Length and fabrication are unrelated. A short form still needs specifics, and the shorter version will still have to invent them under the same instruction.
whyWrong.C: A more capable model follows the same instruction and is at least as fluent at producing convincing detail to satisfy it. This is a specification problem, not a capability problem.
whyWrong.D: Supplying the details is right where they exist. The problem is the fields that are sometimes blank, and the instruction still tells the model to fill them with something.

questions.mindset: 'Be specific' without a source invites invention — say what to do when the information is not supplied.

questions.scenario: A policy analyst has refined a prompt for twenty-five messages. Output has improved on every change she could see, but when she tested it on eight real cases from a different department, two produced answers that failed. The prompt is now 60 lines long.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: She has tuned on one department's cases, so the prompt now carries assumptions specific to those, and length has made those assumptions harder to see and remove.
The prompt has grown too long for the model, so a shorter version should perform better on new cases.
The model has degraded, and the same prompt would have worked a month ago.
Two failures out of eight is within normal variation, so the prompt is probably fine.

questions.explanation: She optimised against **one set of examples**, which is the most common way a well-tuned prompt stops generalising: each change is a good response to a case she was looking at, and together they encode that department's specifics. Sixty lines makes those specifics hard to spot and harder to strip out. The useful move is to work from the two failing cases — find which assumption they break — rather than to keep tuning against the set that already passes.

whyWrong.B: Length is a symptom of accumulating assumptions, not the cause of the failures. Shortening the prompt would not identify which of the accumulated assumptions is wrong for the other department.
whyWrong.C: It assumes a change in the environment rather than in the prompt. Nothing here indicates the tool behaves differently than it did a month ago.
whyWrong.D: Eight cases is a small sample, but the point is not the rate — it is that the failures are real and specific, and those two cases are the most informative examples she has.

questions.mindset: A prompt tuned on one set of cases encodes that set's specifics — the failing cases are where the general rule is missing.

questions.scenario: A support lead's prompt for summarising complaint emails works well. She wants to improve it but is worried about making it worse. She has 30 past complaint emails with the summaries her team accepted.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way for her to iterate from here?

options.text: Keep the current prompt as a baseline, run each candidate change against the same 30 emails, and only keep a change if it improves them without breaking any that already worked.
Rewrite the prompt from scratch with everything she has learned, since a clean prompt avoids carrying forward old structure.
Make several changes at once, since each one is small and the overall direction is what matters.
Ask colleagues to try the revised prompt on live emails for a week and report which replies they had to fix.

questions.explanation: She already holds the thing that makes iteration safe: **a fixed set of real cases with known-acceptable output**. Holding the current prompt as a baseline and changing one thing at a time means every change has to justify itself, and nothing that already worked can quietly break. That is what turns refinement from a series of impressions into a process she can repeat and hand on.

whyWrong.B: Starting over discards what she learned from 30 cases. The current structure is not known to be the problem, and a rewrite has no baseline to be measured against.
whyWrong.C: Changing several things at once makes the result unattributable. If quality moves, she cannot tell which change did it, and if it drops she cannot tell which to undo.
whyWrong.D: Live emails put unverified output in front of customers in exchange for evidence she can already obtain safely from the 30 she has.

questions.mindset: Iterate against a fixed set of real cases, changing one thing at a time, or you cannot tell what worked.

questions.scenario: A sales coordinator's prompt produces proposals that are technically complete but read like a template. She has tried adding 'make it more engaging' twice. Replies come back with more exclamation marks and no change in substance.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely reason this is not working?

options.text: 'Engaging' is a preference rather than a criterion, so the model applies its own interpretation — usually more surface energy. What is needed is a structural change, such as opening with the client's stated problem rather than the company's credentials.
The prompt needs to be much longer, because the model cannot infer tone from a short instruction.
A worked example of an engaging proposal would not help, because the problem is the model's tone rather than the prompt.
The proposals should be shorter, since length is what makes them read like a template.

questions.explanation: 'Engaging' describes a **feeling rather than a test**, so two attempts produced two different interpretations and neither changed the substance — more exclamation marks is what surface energy looks like. The productive move is to make the change structural: specify what the opening must do, and what order the sections take. That is a requirement the output can be judged against, rather than an adjective that can only be interpreted.

whyWrong.B: Length is not the constraint. The proposals are complete and correctly ordered; they simply open the wrong way. More instruction text will not tell the model what engaging means to this team any more clearly than two words did.
whyWrong.C: This rules out the most effective available fix. A worked example would show the pattern directly, and the diagnosis here is about the prompt's vagueness, not about the model being incapable of tone.
whyWrong.D: Template-like writing comes from structure and default phrasing, not from length. Shortening would remove detail without changing how the proposal opens or reads.

questions.mindset: Adjectives cannot be iterated into precision — replace a preference with a structural requirement the output can be judged against.

questions.scenario: A risk analyst must produce a decision briefing for a board that has to choose between two suppliers. She has the two proposals, the cost breakdown, her own scoring notes and three risks she is unsure about. Her first prompt asks for 'a recommendation with pros and cons'.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate emphasis for this request?

options.text: Give the model the decision to make, the criteria that matter and their relative importance, ask for each stated against the evidence with its source, and ask for the uncertainty where the evidence is thin.
Ask for a broad set of ideas so the board sees every angle available before deciding.
Ask for a short, punchy summary, since board papers should be easy to read.
Ask for the strongest case for each supplier in turn, so the board can weigh them itself.

questions.explanation: This is an **analysis task with a decision attached**, so the emphasis is on giving the model the decision, the criteria and their relative weight, and on making the reasoning traceable. Asking for each claim to carry its source turns the briefing from an assertion into something checkable, and asking for the uncertainty is what stops the three unresolved risks being presented as settled. The other emphases each produce output that avoids the question the board has to answer.

whyWrong.B: Broadness suits a task about exploring options, where the value is in seeing what exists. Here the board must choose between two named options, so breadth is scope creep.
whyWrong.C: Brevity is a formatting preference and says nothing about the criteria or the evidence. A short briefing can still be unsupported, and this board is making a commitment.
whyWrong.D: Steelmanning each supplier is legitimate, but it delegates the comparison to the reader and leaves the criteria unstated — which is the part that determines the outcome.

questions.mindset: For a decision briefing, supply the decision, the criteria and their weight, and require each claim to carry its source and its uncertainty.

questions.scenario: A communications officer is drafting an FAQ for residents about a change to a waste collection round. Her prompt asks for 'ten common questions residents might ask'.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate emphasis for this request?

options.text: Derive the questions from the material residents have actually been asking — the service desk logs and the letters received about this round — and answer each from the policy, so the FAQ reflects real concerns.
Ask for the ten most important things residents need to know, listed as headings.
Ask for questions phrased the way a resident would actually speak, so the FAQ sounds approachable.
Ask for a comprehensive FAQ covering every aspect of the service, so nothing is missed.

questions.explanation: The weakness of 'ten common questions' is that **'common' is doing all the work and nobody has specified it** — the model supplies questions it considers typical. The real questions are in the service desk logs and the letters about this round. Deriving from them makes the FAQ match actual concerns, and answering each from the policy keeps the content consistent with what residents will be told. This is a research-shaped task where the source material determines the quality.

whyWrong.B: Asking for the important things to know produces a notice, not an FAQ. Residents arrive with questions rather than needing a list of facts, so the structure does not match the situation.
whyWrong.C: Resident phrasing is worth getting right, but it is not the substantive gap. Without knowing what they are actually asking, the questions are still the model's guesses wearing the right clothes.
whyWrong.D: Comprehensive coverage of the whole service answers questions nobody asked and buries the ones about this change. An FAQ is organised around what people want to know, not around the size of the subject.

questions.mindset: For an FAQ, the questions come from what people have actually asked — 'common questions' is an undefended assumption about what they want.

questions.scenario: A grants officer must tell an unsuccessful applicant why their application was not funded, in a way that is honest, specific and unlikely to generate a complaint. Her prompt asks for 'a polite rejection letter'.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate emphasis for this request?

options.text: Anchor the letter to the specific reasons recorded against that application from the published criteria, state what would have made a difference, and keep the tone respectful without being evasive.
Ask for a warm and encouraging letter, so the applicant is left feeling positive about applying again.
Ask for a short letter that avoids detail, so it is not possible to disagree with.
Ask for a letter that explains the fund's aims and the number of applications received, so the applicant understands why.

questions.explanation: A rejection letter is read adversarially, so what matters is **specificity anchored in the assessment** — the reasons recorded against that application against the published criteria, and what would have changed the outcome. That is what makes it honest and what makes it hard to complain about, because the grounds are the ones already applied. Warmth without specificity is evasion, and vagueness invites a challenge that the organisation then has to answer.

whyWrong.B: Encouragement is not what the letter is for, and warmth without grounds reads as evasive. The applicant cannot tell whether the decision was considered, which is what produces the complaint.
whyWrong.C: Avoiding detail to make a letter unchallengeable is a poor objective, and it removes the applicant's ability to learn. A letter with no reasons invites an appeal rather than preventing one.
whyWrong.D: Explaining the fund's aims and competition is context, not grounds. It leaves the applicant unable to tell what happened to their application, which is the question the letter exists to answer.

questions.mindset: When a message will be read adversarially, ground it in the specific recorded reasons rather than in tone.

questions.scenario: A product team needs a naming shortlist for a new scheduling feature. Their prompt asks for 'ten good names, be creative'.
questions.stem: Which TWO additions would MOST improve the result? Choose TWO.

options.text: State the constraints a name has to satisfy — length, the words it must not resemble, whether a domain is available, and what the name must convey.
Say how many of the ten should be conservative and how many should be genuinely inventive, so the list spans a range.
Ask for the names to be generated one at a time, revising as you go, so quality improves along the way.
Add the names of the ten main competitors, so the shortlist avoids confusing similarity.

questions.explanation: This is an **ideation task where the constraints are the substance**. What the name must and must not satisfy — length, similarity to competitors and to existing products, whether it can be registered, what it has to convey — is what determines whether any candidate is usable, and 'be creative' tells the model none of it. Spanning conservative through inventive is equally useful, because a shortlist of ten identical ideas gives the team no real choice.

whyWrong.C: Generating names one at a time with revision in between is a fine technique for deepening one idea. It does not address the absence of constraints, so it produces ten ideas that are not checked against anything — and it multiplies the effort.
whyWrong.D: Naming competitors helps on similarity, which is one constraint among several, and it is the kind of constraint better stated as a rule than supplied as a list. Length, registrability and what the name must convey are all still unstated.

questions.mindset: In ideation, the constraints are the work — say what a candidate must satisfy and span a range of directions.

questions.scenario: A data team asks Claude to pull specific fields from a 3,000-row CSV export. The headers are internal system names. The team's prompt asks for 'the relevant data'.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: Name the fields wanted, in what order, in what form, and what to do with a row where a value is missing or ambiguous — so the output is consistent enough to use.
Ask for a summary of the file instead, since 3,000 rows is more than anyone will read.
Upload the file to a Project so it is available to the whole team in future.
Ask Claude to decide which fields are relevant, since it can judge better than the team what matters.

questions.explanation: 'The relevant data' hands the selection to the model, which has none of the context for it — it does not know which of the internal field names feed the team's report or what a missing value should become. Naming the fields, the order, the form and the treatment of gaps makes the output usable and repeatable. The gap rule matters most: an unstated handling of missing values is how two runs of the same request produce two different files.

whyWrong.B: A summary of a 3,000-row export is not the deliverable the team asked for. They need fields they can load into a spreadsheet, not a description of the file.
whyWrong.C: Putting the file in a Project solves availability, not selection. The request would still not say which fields are wanted or what to do about gaps.
whyWrong.D: The model cannot judge relevance here because relevance is defined by what the team does with the data. Delegating the selection removes the one part of the request the model cannot infer.

questions.mindset: When you need specific fields, name them — and say what happens to a value that is missing or ambiguous.

questions.scenario: A new starter on a marketing team is building a one-page cheat sheet that pairs each type of work with the prompt emphasis that suits it. She has written one entry: 'Drafting — ask for a creative brief.'
questions.stem: Which pairing is MOST accurate?

options.text: Summarising a long document — name the audience and what they need from it, since a summary is shaped by what it is for.
Drafting from a brief — ask for several distinct options, since a single draft gives nothing to react to.
Brainstorming — state the constraints up front, since constraints are what keep ideas inside the real problem.
Formatting a table — specify the source columns, since the model's choice of layout is rarely what the user wanted.

questions.explanation: Summarising is shaped by purpose, and **the purpose is the thing the requester knows and the model cannot infer** — a summary for a board member and one for an engineer differ in what gets kept. Naming the audience and what they need from it is the emphasis that produces the right summary. The other three describe approaches that either don't apply to the task or are irrelevant to it: a brief already exists when you are drafting from it.

whyWrong.B: The brief is the input, not something to request. And asking for several options is a reasonable drafting technique, but it is not specific to drafting from an existing brief.
whyWrong.C: For brainstorming, constraints do belong in the prompt — which makes this defensible advice attached to the wrong row rather than a wrong principle. The question asks for the most accurate pairing.
whyWrong.D: Giving the source columns matters for extracting data. Layout preference is real but secondary, and this entry would tell someone the wrong thing about which part of the request carries the weight.

questions.mindset: A summary's shape follows its purpose, so name the audience and what they need from it.

questions.scenario: A communications officer has a reliable prompt for the company newsletter. She has to produce the same newsletter monthly. One month the sections come back in a different order, and the previous month's version is in a different chat.
questions.stem: What is the BEST approach for this recurring task?

options.text: Keep the prompt as a saved prompt, and name the section order explicitly in it, so each month's run starts from the same specification rather than from memory.
Continue the same chat each month, so the previous newsletter is in context and the order carries forward.
Reuse the same prompt but add 'use the same section order as last month'.
Ask for the section order to be chosen each month based on which news is most important, so the newsletter stays responsive.

questions.explanation: A recurring task needs a **specification that does not depend on remembering the last run**. A saved prompt gives her one artefact to reuse, and naming the section order inside it removes the dependence entirely — the order is stated, not recalled. The failure in this case is precisely that the order lived in a chat rather than in the specification.

whyWrong.B: This depends on a chat staying open month after month, which is how a newsletter stream becomes unwieldy and how last month's content starts influencing this month's. It also does not give her something reusable to hand to a colleague.
whyWrong.C: Asking the prompt to use last month's order still requires last month to be in context. Nothing in a new chat knows what last month's order was.
whyWrong.D: Varying the order is a legitimate editorial choice and it is not what the reliable template does. Where the order is fixed, saying so in the specification is what makes the output consistent.

questions.mindset: For a recurring task, put everything the output must satisfy into a saved prompt, including anything you would otherwise recall from last time.

questions.scenario: A consultant has been asked to 'understand our business and tell us where AI could help'. She has three weeks, access to a large shared drive, and no specific use case.
questions.stem: Which TWO approaches would MOST improve her chances of a useful answer? Choose TWO.

options.text: Break the work into stages: understand the business and its processes, identify the work that is repetitive or high-volume, assess candidate uses against criteria like volume, error cost and data sensitivity, then recommend a small number with a clear case for each.
Put the business documentation into a Project's knowledge and ask for a comprehensive list of everywhere AI could be used across the organisation.
Ask for a report that maps each department's activities against the tools available, so leadership can pick where to start.
Ask the model to produce its recommendations first and to verify them afterwards, since generating options quickly is the main constraint.

questions.explanation: A brief this broad fails unless it is **staged, with a filter in the middle**. Understanding the business and then assessing candidates against explicit criteria — volume, error cost, data sensitivity, feasibility — is what turns a list of possibilities into a small set of defensible recommendations, and it is what stops a comprehensive answer from being a list of everything imaginable. Verification afterwards is the same idea placed wrongly: it happens after forty recommendations have been generated, so the work of filtering has already happened.

whyWrong.B: This asks for comprehensiveness, which is the failure mode here. Every possible use across an organisation is not a recommendation, and it produces a long list nobody can act on within three weeks.
whyWrong.D: This inverts the order. Generating first and verifying afterwards means the filtering work is done by the reader after a long output, rather than by criteria applied while candidates are being considered.

questions.mindset: A broad brief needs stages with a criteria filter in the middle — generating everything and verifying afterwards just moves the filtering onto the reader.
